paragraphs: Of this: he permitted, on the Sabbath, light carrying, in his saying: "It is not permitted to you to carry except on the [shoulder-]frames" — relying on [Num 7:9]: "אֶלָּא בַּכָּתֵף יִשָּׂאוּ." This is manifestly [self-]undoing. As for [some] of his adherents — they claim that he meant by it carrying within the houses, so that people not be permitted to carry in their houses on their frames. But the plain sense of his words does not indicate what they say — we shall explain this in its place. He permitted prayer only in a defined place, which he calls "the qinyah." He claimed that whoever ate, during "the seven days of unleavened bread," unleavened bread of wheat, was as one who ate leaven. He made circumcision obligatory with scissors and nothing else, and commanded that the milah be done with a "ḥarṣa" — small and large — together with oil of walnut. Whoever departs from these things is, with him, uncircumcised; and likewise one circumcised by a man who does not act so is uncircumcised and must repeat his circumcision. He made the circumcision of an adult obligatory on the eleventh of the month, exclusive of the rest of the days of the month. If a woman wished to enter the religion, she enters on the eighth of the month.
§2 — The month of intercalation; marriage; fasting

He made the seeking of [the barley of] the new-barley (aviv) obligatory on the twenty-fourth of Shevaṭ, claiming that Shevaṭ is the month of intercalation, not Adar. By the plain sense of his statement, he would permit [marriage to] the paternal aunt and the maternal aunt who are not from the [same] father; his adherents flee from this in the utmost flight. He permitted a man to marry the daughter of his father's wife — if his father had no child by her, that is, by her mother; and he claimed that the saying of Scripture [Lev 18:18] "וְאִשָּׁה אֶל אֲחֹתָהּ" means a woman and her sister's daughter. He claimed that the saying of Scripture [Lev 15:8] "וְכִי יָרֹק הַזָּב בַּטָּהוֹר" — that the woman is excluded from it: if a man with a flux spat upon a pure woman, she did not become impure. He made obligatory a fast of seventy days: from the thirteenth of Nisan to the twenty-third of Sivan. He made obligatory the fast of the seventh day of each month, and made obligatory the fast of the day of Esther. He made intercourse obligatory by day, and made it obligatory that a man have intercourse by night and by day more than once. He made intercourse with a pregnant woman obligatory only after she has been [pregnant] three months.
§3 — The month of Nisan; the Festival of Booths; the dead

If the fifteenth of Nisan fell on the Sabbath, he deferred the taking of the festival to Sunday, which is the sixteenth; and likewise for the Festival of Booths. He did not make obligatory the impurity [contracted] from water, and claimed that a [household] vessel does not become impure from a [household] vessel. He brought down the impurity [contracted] from the corpse in this age, and did not make obligatory the impurity from slaughter. He claimed that the mouse of "the two flanks": if it was slaughtered, its impurity was less than the impurity of a corpse. He claimed [a rule concerning] the dead, and that its ruling is the ruling of the menstruant. He made obligatory the impurity only upon one who drew near intentionally; and claimed that the mouse does not convey impurity until it dies on the ground; and claimed that the impure, if he does not immerse from a [household] vessel, is not purified. He permitted the menstruant to stand in the "camp," and permitted the menstruant to discharge [her impurity] in a hollow with earth beneath. He did not permit [the company of] the pure and holy in the religion to one who dissented from him in [even] a single obligation. He made some impurity obligatory only upon one twenty years old, and some upon one five years old. He claimed that the young of a pure beast — if it died before eight days had passed for it — does not convey impurity.

It is reported of him that he held [the doctrine of] "transmigration" (tanāsukh), and that he composed a book on it. We have seen some of his adherents holding this opinion. We shall later recount the statement of those who held transmigration and the passing of souls, and the answer to them.
: The reference for ʿAnan's saying is in Harkavy, Studien und Mittheilungen VIII, p. 69 (and again p. 128), from the Book of Commandments of ʿAnan (a Genizah fragment).
: "the qinyah" — Arabic al-qinyah; perhaps the courtyard of the household. The source is unclear.
: A principal ʿAnanite doctrine: that unleavened bread is valid for Passover only from barley, not wheat. Cf. Ben-Shammai, "Between Ananites and Karaites."
: ʿAnan took Shevaṭ, not Adar, as the month of intercalation — a distinctive ʿAnanite calendar rule. Cf. Vidro (2021).
: A distinctive ʿAnanite fast — seventy days between Nisan and Sivan.
: "the camp" — the camp of Israel; ʿAnan permitted the menstruant in the community, against the rabbinic tradition.
: Arabic al-tanāsukh, the transmigration of souls — a doctrine Q attacks at length in Maqala III.
